=== sources/brindle-docs-3.2.md
# Brindle 3.2 documentation

Brindle is an embeddable message-queue library for Go and Rust services.

## Ordering

Messages are delivered in the order they were published within one queue. The guarantee holds per queue, across all
consumers of that queue, as long as the queue has a single writer.

## Flow control

Each consumer may hold at most 10,000 unacknowledged messages. When a consumer falls further behind, Brindle drops
the oldest unacknowledged message to make room for the new one. The drop is not reported to the publisher or the
consumer; the only trace is the counter `brindle_dropped_total`. Raise `max_unacked` (up to 50,000) or add consumers
if a drop is not acceptable.

## Persistence

Queues are kept in memory and written to a write-ahead log every 200 ms by default (`wal_interval`).

=== sources/quarrel-docs-1.4.md
# Quarrel 1.4 reference

Quarrel is a partitioned message-queue library.

## Delivery

Delivery is at least once. A message that is not acknowledged within `ack_timeout` (30 s by default) is delivered
again, so consumers must be idempotent.

## Ordering

Order is kept within a partition only. A queue is split into 64 partitions by default, and messages of one queue in
different partitions may be delivered in any order. Pin a key to a partition (`partition_key`) to keep the order of
the messages that share it.

## Back-pressure

A publisher blocks when the partition buffer is full; no message is dropped.

final.result:
**Quarrel fits, with one setting. Brindle doesn't fit.**

- **Brindle 3.2:** Ordering is fine: it's per queue, as long as each queue has a single writer. But the "never lose silently" requirement rules it out. When a consumer has more than 10,000 unacknowledged messages (adjustable up to 50,000 via `max_unacked`), Brindle drops the oldest one. Neither the publisher nor the consumer is told; the only trace is the `brindle_dropped_total` counter. Queues also live in memory and are written to disk every 200 ms by default. The docs don't say what happens on a crash, but up to that much recent data could be at risk.
- **Quarrel 1.4:** No message is dropped. When a buffer fills, the publisher waits, and unacknowledged messages are delivered again. That means consumers will sometimes see duplicates, so they must handle the same message twice safely. Ordering is the catch: it only holds within a partition, and a queue is split into 64 partitions by default. To get strict order across a whole queue, give all its messages the same `partition_key` (or use one partition). That gives up parallelism within the queue.

I didn't use two of the sources. The "3x faster" benchmark is from Quarrel's own vendor: one run on a private test setup. The forum post that says Quarrel "never loses a message" has nothing to back it up.

I also saved these findings to the memcue research shelf.
